content.tldr: Kafka outperforms traditional message queues through disk persistence, consumer replayability, zero-copy network transfer, and horizontal partition-level scaling.
content.simple_explanation: Legacy message queues (JMS, RabbitMQ) maintain transient in-memory queues where brokers track individual consumer acknowledgments and delete messages upon delivery. This creates high broker CPU overhead and prevents message replay. Kafka reverses this model: brokers are lightweight append-only log engines, consumers track their own offsets, and disk sequential I/O with page cache zero-copy maximizes throughput while supporting arbitrary consumer replay.
content.real_world_example: A published daily newspaper: the printer prints copies sequentially; whether one reader reads the news at 8 AM or ten readers re-read articles at 6 PM, the printing press does not need to reprint papers for each person.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Decoupling message retention from consumption allows diverse systems (real-time fraud alerting, batch daily data lake ingestion) to consume the exact same event stream without duplicate queues.
